query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Using electrospark deposition (ESPD) with a finer feedstock powder size can overcome the thickness shortfall of the FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock
generation.intervention: Using electrospark deposition (ESPD) with a finer feedstock powder size
generation.conditions: Thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dense and stable oxide layer
generation.mechanism: The ESPD process allows for localized heating with minimal heat input to the substrate, reducing oxidation and alteration of properties. The finer feedstock powder size enables more efficient deposition and improved coating thickness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved coating thickness and preserved coating integrity with minimal as-sprayed oxidation
generation.boundary: Thermal barrier coating system operating conditions
generation.uncertainty: The exact effect of ESPD on the microstructure and properties of the FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat is uncertain and requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Comparative study of FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coats deposited using ESPD with finer feedstock powder size and conventional thermal-spray deposition methods
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ESPD-deposited coating exhibits reduced thickness or increased oxidation compared to the conventional thermal-spray deposition method, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: One of the most promising applications of FeNiCoCrMoAl-based high-entropy alloy is the fabrication of protective coatings. In this work, gas-atomized powder of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 composition was deposited via high-velocity oxygen fuel spraying. It was shown that in-flight oxidation of the powder influences the coating’s phase composition and properties. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, and during continuous heating and prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. Optical and scanning electron microscopy observation, energy dispersive X-ray analysis, X-ray diffraction analysis, thermogravimetric analysis, differential thermal analysis, and microhardness tests were used for study. In a gas-atomized state, the powder consisted of BCC supersaturated solid solution. The high rate of heating and cooling and high oxygen concentration during spraying led to oxidation development prior to decomposition of the supersaturated solid solution. Depleted Al layers of BCC transferred to the FCC phase. Zhao et al.  used a NiCrSiB powder-covered electrode to deposit metal matrix composites (MMC). Recently, electrospark was adopted for alloying Ti-Ni-Zr-Mo-Al-C composite coating on Ti-6Al-4 V surface for higher resistance to wear and high-temperature gas corrosion using metal/alloy powders Ti, Ni, Zr, Mo, Al and Ti3Al + 10%C mixture. These investigations suggest that powders can be one of the feedstocks in coating fabrication, and the “straightforward” combination of M/HEA coatings can be fabricated with ESPD, which could largely simplify the coating process and is readily for new alloy development, yet there is no study related to this approach. In addition to this manufacturing process, the ESPD can rapidly fabricate the M/HEA coating using conventional metal or alloy powder, which can largely reduce the cost, it can neglect the complex surface morphology of the substrate, and it has low requirements to the feedstock in terms of size and shape. The ESPD technique generally exhibits a lower deposition rate compared to other coating methods, making it more suitable for thin coatings.
